title: Modal Verb: können
summary: Talking about ability and possibility with können and infinitive word order.
whyItMatters: The modal verb 'können' lets you say what someone is able to do, what is possible, and whether a proposed time works. It also introduces a central German sentence pattern: a conjugated modal in position two and the main verb as an infinitive at the end.

mentalModel.title: The modal opens a verb frame
mentalModel.content: The conjugated form of 'können' stands near the front, while the activity verb moves to the end: 'Ich kann heute schwimmen.'

mentalModel.title: Conjugate only können
mentalModel.content: The modal changes for the subject. The second verb stays in the infinitive: ich kann spielen, wir können spielen.

mentalModel.title: Ability and possibility share one tool
mentalModel.content: 'Können' can describe skill ('Sie kann gut tanzen') or practical possibility ('Wir können uns am Freitag treffen').

ruleBlocks.title: Conjugate können for the subject
ruleBlocks.content: Use kann with ich and er/sie/es, kannst with du, and können with wir, Sie, and sie. Use könnt with ihr.

ruleBlocks.title: Put the activity infinitive at the end
ruleBlocks.content: In a statement, the conjugated modal is in position two and the main verb remains an infinitive at the end: 'Wir können heute Tennis spielen.'

ruleBlocks.title: Move the modal first in yes-no questions
ruleBlocks.content: Begin a yes-no question with the conjugated modal: 'Kannst du am Samstag kommen?'

ruleBlocks.title: Use nicht to negate ability or possibility
ruleBlocks.content: Place 'nicht' before the final infinitive or near the element being negated: 'Ich kann heute nicht kommen.'

sentenceStructure: The conjugated modal carries person and number.
The main action stays in the infinitive and closes the sentence.
In yes-no questions, the conjugated modal comes first.
In a question with a question word, the modal remains in position two: 'Wann kannst du kommen?'

concepts: conjugate können in the present tense
build statements and questions with a final infinitive
distinguish ability, permission, obligation, and desire
use modal verbs in past and subordinate-clause structures
express nuanced possibilities and polite proposals

comparisons.summary: The theme lesson supplies activities that become the final infinitive in sentences with 'können'.
The communication lesson uses 'können' to propose activities, ask about availability, and reject a time politely.

rows: Wir können uns am Samstag treffen.

examples.de: Wir können am Sonntag Fußball spielen.
examples.en: We can play football on Sunday.

examples.de: Kannst du morgen ins Kino gehen?
examples.en: Can you go to the cinema tomorrow?

examples.de: Heute kann ich leider nicht kommen.

commonMistakes.reason: Only the modal is conjugated; the activity verb stays in the infinitive.
The main infinitive closes the sentence.
A neutral yes-no question begins with the conjugated verb.

specialCases: The singular forms lose the umlaut: ich kann, du kannst, er/sie/es kann.
'Können Sie ...?' is also a common polite request pattern, not only a literal question about ability.
Spoken German can use statement word order with question intonation, but verb-first order is the reliable beginner pattern.
tips: Draw a bracket around the modal and final infinitive in every example.
Practice one sentence through all subjects to learn the irregular forms.
Transform statements into questions by moving the modal before the subject.

memoryHooks.title: Können opens, the action closes
memoryHooks.content: Imagine the modal and infinitive holding the middle of the sentence between them.

memoryHooks.title: One sentence, one conjugated verb
memoryHooks.content: When 'können' is conjugated, the activity verb can relax into its infinitive form.
